L595: To compute the entropy of the Fibonacci polynomials ${M}_{1/n}$ we can use the explicit formula  (16) for the corresponding coefficients ${A}_{i,j}(1/n).$
L596: ###### Proposition 7.3 (Entropy Function for Fibonacci Polynomials). cite10†Image L597: 
L598:  | $$\underset{n\to \mathrm{\infty }}{lim}\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{ln}{A}_{{i}_{n},{j}_{n}}(1/n)=(1-\eta )H\left(\frac{\xi }{1-\eta }\right)+(\xi +\eta )H\left(\frac{\xi }{\xi +\eta }\right),$$  |
L599: 
L600: where $\xi ={lim}_{n\to \mathrm{\infty }}\frac{{i}_{n}}{n},\eta ={lim}_{n\to \mathrm{\infty }}\frac{{j}_{n}}{n}$ and $H$ is given by (29).
L601: ###### Proof.
L602: 
L603: Substituting ${i}_{n}=n{\xi }_{n},{j}_{n}=n{\eta }_{n}$ into Eq. (16) we have
L604: 
L605:  | $${A}_{{i}_{n},{j}_{n}}=\left(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n(1-{\eta }_{n})}{n(1-{\xi }_{n}-{\eta }_{n})}\right)\left(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n({\xi }_{n}+{\eta }_{n})}{n{\eta }_{n}}\right)$$  |
L606: 
L607: and therefore
L608:  | $$\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{ln}{A}_{{i}_{n},{j}_{n}}=\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{ln}\left(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n(1-{\eta }_{n})}{n(1-{\xi }_{n}-{\eta }_{n})}\right)+\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{ln}\left(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n({\xi }_{n}+{\eta }_{n})}{n{\eta }_{n}}\right).$$  |
L609: 
L610: Applying again formula (30) and using the fact that ${\xi }_{n}\to \xi ,{\eta }_{n}\to \eta $ we have
L611:  | $$\underset{n\to \mathrm{\infty }}{lim}\frac{1}{n}\mathrm{ln}{A}_{{i}_{n},{j}_{n}}=(1-\eta )H\left(\frac{\xi }{1-\eta }\right)+(\xi +\eta )H\left(\frac{\xi }{\xi +\eta }\right),$$  |
L612: 
L613: with $H(p)=-p\mathrm{ln}p-(1-p)\mathrm{ln}(1-p)=H(1-p).$ ∎
L614: ###### Theorem 7.4. cite10†Image L615: 
L616: The entropy function of Markov-Fibonacci polynomials
L617: 
L618: (31)  |  | $$ℱ(\xi ,\eta ):=(1-\eta )H\left(\frac{\xi }{1-\eta }\right)+(\xi +\eta )H\left(\frac{\xi }{\xi +\eta }\right)$$  |
L619: 
L620: with $H$ given by (29), is strictly concave on the region $\xi ,\eta >0,\xi +\eta <1$. It is invariant under the change $(\xi ,\eta )\to (\xi ,1-\xi -\eta )$.
L621: ###### Proof.
L622: 
L623: We will prove that the Hessian matrix
L624: 
L625:  | $$\mathrm{Hess}(ℱ)=\left(\begin{array}{cc}{ℱ}_{\xi \xi }& {ℱ}_{\xi \eta }\\ {ℱ}_{\eta \xi }& {ℱ}_{\eta \eta }\end{array}\right)$$  |
L626: 
L627: is negative definite. By Sylvester’s criterion it is enough to show that ${ℱ}_{\xi \xi }<0$ and $det\mathrm{Hess}(ℱ)>0.$ Straightforward calculations lead to
L628:  | $$\mathrm{Hess}(ℱ)=\left(\begin{array}{cc}\frac{1}{\xi +\eta -1}-\frac{2}{\xi }+\frac{1}{\xi +\eta }& \frac{1}{\xi +\eta -1}+\frac{1}{\xi +\eta }\\ \frac{1}{\xi +\eta -1}+\frac{1}{\xi +\eta }& \frac{1}{\xi +\eta -1}+\frac{1}{1-\eta }-\frac{1}{\eta }+\frac{1}{\xi +\eta }\end{array}\right).$$  |
L629: 
L630: Clearly ${ℱ}_{\xi \xi }<0$ since $\frac{1}{\xi +\eta -1}<0$ and $\frac{1}{\xi }>\frac{1}{\xi +\eta }>0$. Computing the determinant and simplifying we find
L631:  | $$det\mathrm{Hess}(ℱ)=\frac{1}{\eta (\xi +\eta )(1-\eta )(1-\xi -\eta )},$$  |
L632: 
L633: where all terms in the denominator are positive in the specified region and hence the determinant is positive as required. Therefore the function is strictly concave.
L634: 
L635: The symmetry $(\xi ,\eta )\to (\xi ,1-\xi -\eta )$ is evident from formula (31). ∎
L636: The graph of the corresponding function $ℱ(\xi ,\eta )$ is shown in Figure 10. The maximum value is $2\mathrm{ln}\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$ achieved at $\xi =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},\eta =\frac{5-\sqrt{5}}{10}.$

L639: ## cite9†Image 8 Critical triangle and Markov sails cite10†Image L640: 
L641: We can split up the Newton polygon by drawing ‘critical lines’ $i=a,j=b$ as shown in Figure 11. The set of lattice points with
L642: 
L643:  | $$i<a,j<b,\frac{i}{a}+\frac{j}{b}>1$$  |
L644: 
L645: we will refer to as the critical triangle.
L646: 
L647: Figure 11. Critical triangle of the weighted Newton polygon ${\mathrm{\Delta }}_{29}$. Notice that per our definition, the lines $i=2$ and $j=3$ themselves are not considered as part of the critical triangle.
L648: In this section we will look at Markov coefficients inside the critical triangle in more detail. We begin with the following conjecture based on the analysis of experimental data.
L649: ###### Conjecture 8.1. cite10†Image L650: 
L651: (Factor 4 Conjecture) The coefficients of Markov polynomials strictly within the critical triangle are divisible by 4.
L652: 
L653: We are going to be more specific about the coefficients on the lower boundary of the critical triangle, using the following geometric interpretation of continued fractions proposed by Felix Klein.
L654: Take the region $[0,a]\times [0,b]$ for some positive integers $a,b$ and divide it into two parts with the line $y=\frac{b}{a}x$. Then consider the convex hull of integer points in each of the two parts, the boundary either side of the line $y=\frac{b}{a}x$ will be a broken line that is called, following Arnold, the sail (see [2, 18]). More precisely,
L655: 
L656:   * •
L657: The vertices on the sail containing the point $(1,0)$ are defined to be ${A}_{0},{A}_{1},\mathrm{\dots },{A}_{n}$ (where ${A}_{0}=(1,0)$). This is the lower sail (i.e., below the line).
L658: 
L659:   * •
L660: 
L661: The vertices on the sail containing the point $(0,1)$ are defined to be ${B}_{0},{B}_{1},\mathrm{\dots },{B}_{n}$ (where ${B}_{0}=(0,1)$). This is the upper sail (i.e., above the line).
L662: One can prove that these vertices on the sails can be found as the convergents of the continued fraction for $\frac{b}{a}$ (see for example [18]).
L663: In particular, we have the following procedure to find the Klein diagram. Plot points $({q}_{k},{p}_{k})$ to represent the continuants ${C}_{k}$ alongside the line $y=\frac{b}{a}x$, then connect with straight lines the the points $({q}_{k},{p}_{k})$ and $({q}_{k+2},{p}_{k+2})$. Note that the points representing even-indexed continuants will all lie above the line $y=\frac{b}{a}x$ whilst the odd-indexed ones will lie below.
L664: ###### Example 8.2. cite10†Image L665: 
L666: Consider the rational $\frac{5}{3}=[1,1,2]$, its continuants are given in the following table.
L667: 
L668:  |  |  | 1  | 1  | 2
L669: --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---
L670: ${p}_{k}$  | 0  | 1  | 1  | 2  | 5
L671: ${q}_{k}$  | 1  | 0  | 1  | 1  | 3
L672: 
L673: (${C}_{-1}=\frac{0}{1},{C}_{0}=\frac{1}{0},{C}_{1}=\frac{1}{1},{C}_{2}=\frac{2}{1},{C}_{3}=\frac{5}{3}$).

L675: Figure 12. Klein Diagram for the rational $\frac{5}{3}$

L677: More formally we can define ${A}_{i}$’s and ${B}_{i}$’s as follows,
L678: (32)  |  | $${A}_{i}=({q}_{2i-1},{p}_{2i-1}),{B}_{i}=({q}_{2i},{p}_{2i}),$$  |
L679: 
L680: where $\frac{{p}_{k}}{{q}_{k}}=[{a}_{1},{a}_{2},\mathrm{\dots },{a}_{k}]$ is the $k$th convergent. Note that for rationals we always consider the final continuant (i.e., the point $(a,b)$) to be part of both sails.
L681: There may be more integer points lying on the sail, indeed in the Example 8.2 the point $(2,3)$ lies on the line between ${A}_{1}$ and ${A}_{2}$. These additional integer points can actually be found immediately if we instead look at the convergents of the Hirzebruch (negative) continued fraction instead, as it was shown by Ustinov in [32].
L682: 
L683: From the theory of continued fractions, we know
L684: 
L685:  | $${p}_{k}={a}_{k}{p}_{k-1}+{p}_{k-2},{q}_{k}={a}_{k}{q}_{k-1}+{p}_{k-2}.$$  |
L686: This means that the line joining the second-last convergent’s coordinates $({p}_{k-2},{q}_{k-2})$ to the corner will have gradient equal to the penultimate convergent. This means that if we flip one of the sails, so that they are both on the same side of the diagonal, they will intersect at the point corresponding to the final convergent. In this way we can combine the sails onto one side.
L687: More explicitly, if we consider the coordinate system of the lower sail (blue) to have origin at $(a,b)$ and directions reversed from normal then we can connect the sails. In practise, continuing on from Example 8.2 this is shown on the left in Figure 13.
L688: Figure 13. (Left) Combined sail for the rational $\frac{5}{3}$; (Right) the reflection in the line $x=a/2$.
L689: 
L690: This is precisely the convex hull of the integer lattice above the line $y=\frac{b}{a}x$ (with endpoints $(0,0),(3,5)$ omitted).
L691: 
L692: From Eq. (11) it is clear to see that the critical triangle of the Newton polygon consists of a region $[0,a]\times [0,b]$ split via a central diagonal, which is comparable to that of the Klein diagram. Furthermore, we are again only interested in integral points.
L693: Indeed, reflecting the leftmost picture in Figure 13 in the line $x=\frac{a}{2}$ we obtain the critical triangle, where coordinate frames have been shown in their corresponding colours.
L694: 
L695: The integer points on this combined sail all refer to a monomial in the Markov polynomial and as such they each have their own coefficient. We will refer to this combined sail, together with the coefficients at each point as the Markov sail.
L696: With our change of coordinate frames, we reformulate the definition of points from Eq. (32) to
L697: 
L698:  | $$\stackrel{~}{{A}_{i}}=({q}_{2i-1},b-{p}_{2i-1}),\stackrel{~}{{B}_{i}}=(a-{q}_{2i},{p}_{2i}),$$  |
L699: 
L700: but going forward we will omit the tilde’s for simplicity.
L701: ### cite8†Image 8.1 Markov Sail Duality cite10†Image L702: 
L703: There is an important Edge-Angle duality between the two sails, saying that the length of a unbroken line on one sail is equal to the ‘index’ at a vertex/rational angle on the opposite sail, see Karpenkov [18].
L704: Here the integer length (denoted $\text{l}\mathrm{\ell }(AB)$) of a line segment $AB$ is defined to be the number of integer points on the its interior plus $1$, and the index (denoted $\text{l}\alpha (\mathrm{\angle }BAC)$) of a rational angle $\mathrm{\angle }BAC$ is defined to be the index of the sublattice generated by the integer vectors of the lines $AB$ and $AC$ in the integer lattice, see [18].
L705: 
L706: Formally, Karpenkov stated this duality as follows
L707:  | $\text{l}\alpha (\mathrm{\angle }{A}_{i}{A}_{i+1}{A}_{i+2})=\text{l}\mathrm{\ell }({B}_{i}{B}_{i+1})$  | $={a}_{2i+2},$  |
L708:  | $\text{l}\alpha (\mathrm{\angle }{B}_{i}{B}_{i+1}{B}_{i+2})=\text{l}\mathrm{\ell }({A}_{i+1}{A}_{i+2})$  | $={a}_{2i+3},$  |
L709: 
L710: where ${a}_{i}$’s are the partial quotients of the continued fraction $\frac{b}{a}=[{a}_{1},{a}_{2},\mathrm{\dots }]$.
L711: We conjecture that in our case (for the so called Markov sails) we have a sort of duality between the ‘weights’ of these vertices/lines on the sail. Denote $ℳ(C)$ to be the coefficient of the monomial represented at the point $C$ on the Newton polygon, we will refer to these as $ℳ$-values and define this only for integer points in the interior of the critical triangle (i.e., not on the boundary).
L712: It appears as though, on unbroken lines of the sail, the coefficients differ according to an arithmetic progression. Denote $d({C}_{i}{C}_{i+1})$ to be the common difference of $ℳ$-values of integer points along an unbroken line segment of the Markov sail between vertices ${C}_{i}$ and ${C}_{i+1}$. We conjecture the following extended duality.
L713: ###### Conjecture 8.3.
L714: 
L715: (Markov Sail Duality) The coefficients of Markov polynomials satisfy Markov sail duality
L716: 
L717:  | $d({B}_{i}{B}_{i+1})$  | $=-ℳ({A}_{i+1})$  |
